title: Heart Valves and the Cardiac Cycle
subject: Cardiovascular System (CARD)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter follows the four heart valves through one heartbeat. It covers valve structure and auscultation sites, the Wiggers diagram, the left ventricular pressure-volume loop, the jugular venous pulse, the heart sounds, and the timing of murmurs and their response to bedside maneuvers. One principle explains all of it: a valve is passive, opening when the pressure behind it exceeds the pressure in front of it and closing when that gradient reverses. Board questions give a tracing, a loop, a neck vein finding, or an auscultation description and ask for the phase, the valve, or the lesion. Knowing which two pressures are compared at each moment, and how a lesion or maneuver changes them, answers most of these questions.

terms.def: The tricuspid or mitral valve, which separates an atrium from its ventricle and is anchored by chordae tendineae to papillary muscles.
The pulmonary or aortic valve, made of three pocket-shaped cusps without chordae, which separates a ventricle from its great artery.
Fibrous cords that connect the free edges and ventricular surfaces of AV valve cusps to papillary muscles.
The first part of systole, when the ventricle contracts with all valves closed, so pressure rises while volume does not change.
The first part of diastole, when the ventricle relaxes with all valves closed, so pressure falls while volume does not change.
The small downward deflection and rebound on the aortic pressure curve at the moment the aortic valve closes.
A plot of ventricular pressure against ventricular volume through one beat, whose width is the stroke volume and whose area is the stroke work.
The pulsation of the internal jugular vein, which reflects right atrial pressure and its waves.
A very large jugular a wave produced when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve.
The aortic and pulmonic components of the second heart sound, produced by closure of each semilunar valve.
A low-pitched early diastolic sound produced when rapid inflow into a ventricle is abruptly decelerated.
A low-pitched late diastolic sound produced when atrial contraction forces blood into a stiff ventricle.

sections.title: Valve structure, chordae and papillary muscles, and auscultation areas

blocks.text: The two atrioventricular (AV) valves separate atria from ventricles, and the two semilunar valves separate ventricles from the great arteries. All four attach to the fibrous skeleton, dense connective tissue rings (anuli fibrosi) that hold the openings in shape and electrically insulate the atria from the ventricles. Each cusp is a fold of endocardium with a connective tissue core and no muscle, so valve motion is entirely passive and follows the pressure gradient across it.
Atrioventricular valves

The tricuspid valve has anterior, posterior, and septal cusps; the mitral valve has anterior and posterior cusps. The larger anterior mitral cusp lies between left ventricular inflow and outflow, in fibrous continuity with the aortic valve. In systole, high ventricular pressure would evert the large, thin AV cusps into the atria. Chordae tendineae tether the cusp edges to papillary muscles, which contract with the ventricle and keep the chordae taut as it shortens. Each papillary muscle sends chordae to two adjacent cusps, so contraction pulls their edges together. Papillary muscles therefore hold the AV valves shut in systole; they do not pull them open in diastole.

The right ventricle has anterior, posterior, and septal papillary muscles; the anterior one receives the moderator band, which carries the right bundle branch. The left ventricle has anterolateral and posteromedial muscles. The anterolateral muscle usually has a dual supply (left anterior descending and circumflex branches), whereas the posteromedial muscle usually depends on the posterior descending artery alone, which arises from the right coronary artery in most hearts. Inferior infarction can therefore rupture the posteromedial muscle.

blocks.title: Papillary muscle rupture after inferior infarction
steps: Occlusion of the right coronary or posterior descending artery
Necrosis of the posteromedial papillary muscle (single blood supply)
Rupture of the softened muscle, usually within the first week
Mitral cusps flail into the left atrium in systole
Acute severe mitral regurgitation into a small, noncompliant atrium
Large v waves, pulmonary edema, and low forward stroke volume
blocks.caption: Ruptured chordae from myxomatous disease or endocarditis cause the same loss of support. Acute regurgitation is poorly tolerated because the atrium has not dilated.

blocks.text: Semilunar valves and auscultation areas

The pulmonary and aortic valves have three pocket-shaped cusps without chordae. Backflow at the end of systole fills the pockets and presses the cusps together, and a central nodule with thin lateral lunules on each cusp seals the valve. The coronary arteries arise from the right and left aortic sinuses behind the cusps, giving the names right coronary, left coronary, and noncoronary cusps. A bicuspid aortic valve, present in about 1% to 2% of people, calcifies and becomes stenotic early.

blocks.title: Comparison of the four heart valves
rows: Left lower sternal border, 4th to 5th intercostal space
Chordae to anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles
Apex, left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line
Right, left, posterior (right coronary, left coronary, noncoronary)
blocks.caption: AV valves need chordae because their large cusps face high systolic pressure; semilunar valves seal by the shape of their cusps.

blocks.text: The valves lie close together behind the sternum, so each is heard where its sound is carried, downstream or over the nearest chamber. Aortic sounds follow the ascending aorta to the right second intercostal space, so aortic stenosis radiates to the carotids. Pulmonary sounds follow the pulmonary trunk to the left second space. Tricuspid sounds are heard over the right ventricle, which forms most of the anterior heart surface. Mitral sounds are heard at the apex, and mitral regurgitation radiates to the left axilla along the backward jet.

sections.title: The Wiggers diagram: pressure gradients, valve events, and S1 and S2

blocks.text: The Wiggers diagram plots left atrial, left ventricular, and aortic pressures, LV volume, the ECG, and heart sounds against time. Every valve event is a crossing of two pressure curves, so reading it means asking which pressure across each valve is higher. At about 75 beats per minute a cycle lasts about 0.8 s (systole about 0.3 s, diastole about 0.5 s). Faster rates shorten diastole far more than systole, reducing filling time and left ventricular coronary perfusion, which occurs mainly in diastole.
Systole

Shortly after the QRS complex the ventricle contracts. When LV pressure exceeds LA pressure the mitral valve closes, then the tricuspid, producing S1 (best at the apex) from vibration of the tensed cusps, chordae, walls, and blood. During isovolumetric contraction (about 0.05 s) all valves are closed and pressure rises at constant volume until it exceeds aortic diastolic pressure (about 80 mmHg) and the aortic valve opens. Opening is silent unless a stiff, domed valve produces an ejection click.

About two thirds of the stroke volume leaves during rapid ejection, as ventricular and aortic pressures peak at about 120 mmHg. In reduced ejection the T wave begins and LV pressure falls slightly below aortic pressure while momentum carries blood forward. When flow briefly reverses, the aortic valve closes, and the backflow and aortic rebound produce the dicrotic notch. Volume falls from an end-diastolic volume (EDV) of about 120 mL to an end-systolic volume (ESV) of about 50 mL: stroke volume about 70 mL, ejection fraction about 55% to 70%. Pulmonary artery pressure is about 25/8 mmHg.
Diastole

Aortic then pulmonic closure produces S2, best heard at the base. During isovolumetric relaxation all valves are closed and pressure falls at constant volume while the atria fill. When LV pressure drops below LA pressure the mitral valve opens and rapid filling, aided by active relaxation, delivers most of the filling. Reduced filling (diastasis) follows and is the part lost first as heart rate rises. Atrial contraction after the P wave supplies about the last 20% of EDV at rest, a share that grows at fast rates and in stiff ventricles.

blocks.title: Valve events in one left-sided cardiac cycle
steps: Atrial systole completes filling to EDV
LV pressure exceeds LA pressure: mitral valve closes (S1)
Isovolumetric contraction: all valves closed, pressure rises
LV pressure exceeds aortic pressure (about 80 mmHg): aortic valve opens
Rapid then reduced ejection: volume falls to ESV
Flow reverses: aortic valve closes (S2, dicrotic notch)
Isovolumetric relaxation: all valves closed, pressure falls
LV pressure falls below LA pressure: mitral valve opens
Rapid filling (S3 if present), then diastasis
blocks.caption: Each valve event is a pressure crossover; only the isovolumetric phases have all valves closed.

blocks.text: Right heart timing and S1 intensity

The right heart follows the same sequence at lower pressures. The pulmonary valve opens before the aortic valve, since the right ventricle needs only about 8 mmHg to exceed pulmonary diastolic pressure, and closes after it, since the low-impedance pulmonary circulation prolongs forward flow; A2 therefore precedes P2. S1 is loud with a short PR interval or mitral stenosis (cusps still wide open when contraction starts) and soft with a long PR interval.

blocks.title: Identifying the phase from pressures
blocks.text: A tracing shows left atrial pressure 8 mmHg, left ventricular pressure 50 mmHg, aortic pressure 82 mmHg, and LV volume 120 mL. Step 1: LV pressure exceeds LA pressure, so the mitral valve is closed. Step 2: aortic pressure exceeds LV pressure, so the aortic valve is closed. Step 3: with both valves closed volume cannot change, and 120 mL is the end-diastolic volume. This is isovolumetric contraction, and S1 has just occurred. If the same pressure relationships appear with a volume of 50 mL, the ventricle is at end-systolic volume, so the phase is isovolumetric relaxation just after S2. Volume, not pressure, separates the two isovolumetric phases.

sections.title: The left ventricular pressure-volume loop and its changes in valve disease

blocks.text: The pressure-volume loop plots LV pressure against LV volume for one beat, traced counterclockwise. At the bottom right corner (EDV about 120 mL, about 8 mmHg) the mitral valve closes. The right side is vertical: isovolumetric contraction. At the top right corner (about 80 mmHg) the aortic valve opens, and the top of the loop is ejection, peaking near 120 mmHg. At the top left corner (ESV about 50 mL, about 100 mmHg) the aortic valve closes. The left side is vertical isovolumetric relaxation, the mitral valve opens at the bottom left corner, and the bottom edge is filling with little rise in pressure in a compliant ventricle.

The width (EDV minus ESV) is stroke volume and the enclosed area is stroke work. The bottom edge follows the end-diastolic pressure-volume relationship, which is steeper in a stiff ventricle, and the top left corner lies on the end-systolic pressure-volume line, whose slope rises with contractility (CV-6).
Valve lesions

In aortic stenosis the ventricle must generate far more pressure than the aorta to eject, so the loop is tall, with peak LV pressures of about 180 to 250 mmHg while aortic pressure stays normal or low. Incomplete ejection raises ESV and narrows the loop. Concentric hypertrophy normalizes wall stress but stiffens the ventricle, steepening the diastolic edge and raising end-diastolic pressure. The extra loop area means greater stroke work and oxygen demand.

In aortic regurgitation blood leaks back from the aorta as soon as ventricular pressure falls, so volume rises during what should be isovolumetric relaxation. Filling from both atrium and aorta makes EDV very large, and the Frank-Starling mechanism produces a large total stroke volume. Systolic pressure rises, diastolic aortic pressure falls, and pulse pressure widens. Chronic eccentric hypertrophy (sarcomeres added in series) makes the ventricle more compliant, shifting the loop right.

In mitral regurgitation blood escapes into the left atrium as soon as LV pressure exceeds LA pressure, long before the aortic valve opens, so volume falls during what should be isovolumetric contraction. The low-pressure atrium is a second outlet, so ESV tends to fall early in the disease, and the regurgitant volume returns next diastole, raising EDV. Total stroke volume rises but forward output falls. Mitral stenosis, by contrast, underfills the ventricle, so the loop becomes small and shifted left.

blocks.title: Pressure-volume loop changes in three valve lesions
rows: Greatly increased; LV to aortic gradient
Wide, shifted right, left side slopes
Wide, shifted right, right side slopes
blocks.caption: A regurgitant lesion abolishes the isovolumetric phase in which the leaking valve should be closed.

blocks.title: Reading a lesion from the loop
blocks.text: A loop shows EDV 200 mL, ESV 70 mL, and peak pressure 110 mmHg, and volume starts falling at the bottom right corner while pressure is only about 15 mmHg. Step 1: stroke volume is 130 mL, far above 70 mL, so there is a volume load. Step 2: the ventricle loses volume before its pressure could open the aortic valve, so blood is leaving backward through an incompetent mitral valve. Step 3: peak pressure is not raised, which argues against aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation. The answer is mitral regurgitation. A loop whose left side slopes to the right, gaining volume while pressure falls after ejection, is filling from the aorta: aortic regurgitation.

sections.title: The jugular venous pulse: a, c, and v waves and x and y descents

blocks.text: The right internal jugular vein runs nearly straight through the brachiocephalic vein and superior vena cava into the right atrium, so right atrial pressure changes appear as neck pulsations. Pulsation height estimates right atrial pressure: the sternal angle lies about 5 cm above the right atrium, so with the patient at about 45 degrees, a pulsation more than about 3 cm above the sternal angle suggests raised pressure. Unlike the carotid pulse, the jugular pulse is not palpable, usually shows two peaks per cycle, falls with inspiration, and changes with position. The left atrial (wedge) tracing has the same waves.
Waves and descents

The a wave is right atrial contraction, after the P wave and just before S1. The c wave, just after S1, occurs as the closed tricuspid valve bulges into the atrium during right ventricular isovolumetric contraction, with some transmitted carotid pulsation. The x descent is the systolic fall in atrial pressure from atrial relaxation and the downward pull of the tricuspid ring as the ventricle ejects. The v wave is atrial filling from the venae cavae against the closed tricuspid valve, peaking near S2. The y descent is atrial emptying when the tricuspid valve opens, during rapid filling.
Abnormal waves

Cannon a waves occur when the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve, forcing its contraction backward into the neck. In complete heart block, ventricular tachycardia with AV dissociation, and ventricular pacing, atria and ventricles beat independently, so cannon waves appear irregularly on beats when timing coincides. When atria and ventricles activate together on every beat, as in some junctional rhythms and AV nodal reentrant tachycardia, they appear regularly. Large but not cannon a waves reflect resistance to atrial emptying through an open valve, as in tricuspid stenosis or a stiff right ventricle. The a wave disappears in atrial fibrillation.

In tricuspid regurgitation the atrium also receives blood ejected backward from the right ventricle, so pressure rises throughout systole. The x descent is lost, c and v merge into a large systolic c-v wave, the y descent is steep, and systolic hepatic pulsation may be felt. Acute mitral regurgitation produces the same large v wave on the wedge tracing.

blocks.predict: A 74-year-old with syncope has a regular pulse of 38 beats per minute. Looking at the neck, you see occasional very large venous pulsations that do not occur with every beat. What is the mechanism, and why are they intermittent?
blocks.explain: This is complete heart block with independent atrial and ventricular rhythms. When a P wave falls during ventricular systole, the right atrium contracts against a closed tricuspid valve and produces a cannon a wave. Because the rhythms are unrelated, the coincidence occurs only on some beats.
blocks.check: Compare with the cannon a wave paragraph and AV dissociation in CV-7.

sections.title: Physiologic, wide, fixed, and paradoxical splitting of S2

blocks.text: S2 has an aortic component (A2), loud and heard widely, and a pulmonic component (P2), soft and best heard at the left second intercostal space, where splitting is assessed. A2 normally comes first. A split is audible when the components are more than about 0.03 s apart.
Physiologic splitting

Inspiration increases venous return to the right heart and lowers pulmonary impedance, so right ventricular ejection lasts longer and P2 is delayed. The expanded pulmonary vessels briefly hold more blood, so left ventricular filling dips and A2 comes slightly earlier. The split widens to about 0.04 s on inspiration and closes in expiration. It is most easily heard in children and young adults.

blocks.title: Physiologic splitting of S2 during inspiration
steps: Inspiration: intrathoracic pressure becomes more negative
Systemic venous return to the right heart rises
RV ejection lasts longer
Pulmonary vascular impedance falls, prolonging forward flow
P2 is delayed
Blood pools in the lungs, LV filling dips, A2 comes slightly earlier
The split widens
blocks.caption: Breathing changes right heart filling more than left, so the split widens on inspiration and narrows on expiration.

blocks.text: Abnormal splitting

Wide splitting is present in expiration and widens further on inspiration, because P2 is late throughout while the respiratory mechanism still works. In right bundle branch block the right ventricle is activated late; in pulmonic stenosis its ejection is prolonged. Severe mitral regurgitation gives the left ventricle a second outlet, shortening ejection and moving A2 earlier.

Fixed splitting, classically from an atrial septal defect, is wide and does not change with breathing. The left-to-right shunt volume-loads the right ventricle and distends the pulmonary bed, delaying P2. Because the atria act as one chamber, the extra systemic return of inspiration is offset by a smaller shunt, and the reverse occurs in expiration, so right ventricular volume and P2 timing stay nearly constant.

Paradoxical splitting occurs when A2 is delayed past P2. The split is heard in expiration and narrows or disappears on inspiration, as the normal delay of P2 moves it toward the late A2. A2 is delayed electrically in left bundle branch block and right ventricular pacing, and mechanically in severe aortic stenosis and obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

blocks.title: Patterns of S2 splitting
rows: Inspiration delays P2 and slightly advances A2
Right bundle branch block, pulmonic stenosis; severe mitral regurgitation (early A2)
Constant RV volume load; shunt changes offset changes in venous return
Left bundle branch block, severe aortic stenosis, right ventricular pacing
blocks.caption: Ask two questions: is a split heard in expiration, and does inspiration widen it, leave it unchanged, or narrow it?

sections.title: S3 and S4, and functional flow murmurs

blocks.text: S3 and S4 are low-pitched diastolic sounds made by the ventricle and its blood, not by valves. Left-sided sounds are heard best with the bell at the apex in the left lateral position; right-sided sounds at the left lower sternal border, louder on inspiration.
S3: a volume sound

S3 occurs in early diastole, about 0.12 to 0.16 s after S2, during rapid filling. A large, fast inflow is suddenly decelerated as the ventricle reaches its limit of expansion, setting the walls and blood vibrating. It is often normal in children, young adults up to about age 40, trained athletes, and pregnancy, where a compliant ventricle fills briskly. In older adults it signals volume overload: a dilated failing ventricle with high atrial pressure, regurgitant volume returning in mitral or aortic regurgitation, a left-to-right shunt, or a high-output state. Significant mitral stenosis prevents rapid filling and therefore an S3. S3 can persist in atrial fibrillation.
S4: a stiffness sound

S4 occurs in late diastole just before S1, with atrial contraction. Atrial ejection into a stiff ventricle causes a sharp rise in pressure and a low-frequency vibration. It indicates reduced compliance: hypertrophy from hypertension, aortic stenosis, or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and acute ischemia, which impairs relaxation. It may occur with age-related stiffening but is abnormal in the young. Because it requires atrial contraction, S4 is absent in atrial fibrillation.

blocks.predict: A 68-year-old with long-standing hypertension and left ventricular hypertrophy has a late diastolic sound just before S1. A month later the ECG shows atrial fibrillation and the sound is gone, although the hypertrophy is unchanged. Why did the sound disappear?
blocks.explain: The sound was an S4, produced by atrial contraction into the stiff hypertrophied ventricle. In atrial fibrillation there is no organized atrial contraction, so the sound disappears even though the ventricle is no more compliant.

blocks.text: Functional flow murmurs

A murmur is turbulent flow. Turbulence appears when the Reynolds number, which rises with velocity and vessel diameter and falls with viscosity, exceeds a critical value. A normal valve can therefore produce a murmur when flow is high or blood is thin. In pregnancy, blood volume rises about 40% to 50% and cardiac output about 30% to 50%. In anemia, hypoxic vasodilation raises cardiac output and low red cell mass reduces viscosity. Fever, thyrotoxicosis, and exercise raise output. Removing the cause removes the murmur.

Children commonly have innocent murmurs because of a thin chest wall and high output relative to size: a vibratory, musical early systolic murmur at the left lower sternal border or apex (Still murmur), a soft pulmonary flow murmur, and the venous hum, a continuous murmur above the clavicle that disappears when the child lies down or the jugular vein is compressed. Functional murmurs are soft (grade 1 or 2, no thrill), early to mid systolic ejection murmurs at the base or left sternal border, with normal S2 splitting and no extra sounds. A diastolic or holosystolic murmur, a thrill, or an abnormal S2 points to structural disease; the venous hum is the exception.

sections.title: Classifying murmurs by timing and location, and their response to maneuvers

blocks.text: A murmur's timing and shape follow the time course of the pressure gradient that drives it. Intensity is graded 1 (faint) to 6 (heard with the stethoscope off the chest); a palpable thrill means grade 4 or higher.
Systolic murmurs

Ejection murmurs arise across the aortic or pulmonic outflow. Flow begins only after isovolumetric contraction, so the murmur starts after S1, peaks with ejection velocity, and ends before S2. In aortic stenosis, as severity increases, the peak moves later and A2 softens.

Holosystolic murmurs (mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, ventricular septal defect) arise when blood escapes into a lower-pressure chamber from the onset of contraction, so they run evenly from S1 to S2; a small septal defect may be loud because its jet is fast. In mitral valve prolapse the cusps hold until the ventricle becomes small enough in mid systole, so a midsystolic click precedes a late systolic murmur.
Diastolic and continuous murmurs

In aortic regurgitation the backward gradient is greatest right after the valve should close, so a high-pitched decrescendo murmur starts at A2, best heard sitting forward in held expiration; pulmonic regurgitation, usually from pulmonary hypertension, is similar. In mitral stenosis flow begins only when high atrial pressure snaps the valve open (opening snap), followed by a low rumble. Worse stenosis means higher atrial pressure and earlier opening, so a shorter S2 to opening snap interval means more severe disease. In patent ductus arteriosus aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary pressure throughout the cycle, giving a continuous murmur.

blocks.title: Classification of murmurs by timing
rows: Click earlier when LV is smaller
blocks.caption: Stenosis is heard when the valve should be open, regurgitation when it should be closed.

blocks.text: Dynamic maneuvers

Maneuvers change preload, afterload, or both. Most murmurs grow louder with more preload, and regurgitant murmurs with more afterload. Handgrip raises afterload, increasing backflow in mitral regurgitation, aortic regurgitation, and ventricular septal defect while reducing the aortic stenosis gradient. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and mitral valve prolapse move opposite to most murmurs with preload. Valsalva strain or standing lowers venous return and shrinks the ventricle, bringing the hypertrophied septum and anterior mitral cusp closer and worsening outflow obstruction, and letting redundant mitral cusps prolapse earlier. In aortic stenosis the obstruction is fixed, so lower preload only reduces flow and softens the murmur.

blocks.title: Effects of maneuvers on murmurs
rows: MR, AR, VSD louder; AS softer
blocks.caption: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and mitral valve prolapse worsen as the left ventricular cavity shrinks.

blocks.predict: A patient with a midsystolic click and late systolic apical murmur stands up quickly from a squat. Predict the change in the click and murmur.
blocks.explain: The click moves earlier and the murmur lengthens. Standing reduces venous return, so the ventricle starts systole smaller and the redundant cusps prolapse earlier in contraction.

integration.text: The valves form from endocardial cushions, so cushion defects produce AV septal defects and abnormal valves together (CV-1), and the fibrous skeleton that anchors them also separates atrial from ventricular conduction (CV-7). Physiology ties every finding to pressure gradients: the Wiggers diagram, the pressure-volume loop, the jugular pulse, and the heart sounds are four views of valves opening when upstream pressure is higher. Preload, afterload, and contractility (CV-6) change those gradients, which is why breathing and maneuvers alter splitting and murmurs. Pathology supplies the causes (CV-18-D): calcific and bicuspid aortic stenosis, rheumatic mitral disease after group A streptococcal infection through cross-reactive immunity, endocarditis, and myxomatous degeneration in mitral valve prolapse and in Marfan syndrome (fibrillin-1) or Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (collagen). Whether a lesion imposes a pressure or a volume load predicts concentric or eccentric hypertrophy.

Auscultation has limits. Loudness depends on flow as well as severity, so a severely stenotic valve may soften as cardiac output falls and a small ventricular septal defect may be louder than a large one. Obesity and emphysema muffle sounds. Bedside findings identify the likely lesion and its mechanism, while imaging and pressure measurement define severity.

summary: Valves move passively: each opens when the pressure behind it exceeds the pressure in front of it and closes when the gradient reverses.

Papillary muscles hold AV cusps shut in systole; the posteromedial muscle usually has a single supply from the posterior descending artery, so inferior infarction can rupture it and cause acute mitral regurgitation.
Aortic sounds are heard at the right 2nd intercostal space, pulmonic at the left 2nd, tricuspid at the left lower sternal border, and mitral at the apex.
S1 is AV valve closure at the start of isovolumetric contraction and S2 is semilunar closure at the start of isovolumetric relaxation; only these phases have all valves closed.
Normal LV values are about 120 mL EDV, 50 mL ESV, 70 mL stroke volume, and ejection fraction 55% to 70%; atrial contraction supplies about 20% of filling at rest.

The counterclockwise pressure-volume loop has stroke volume as its width; aortic stenosis makes it tall, aortic regurgitation removes isovolumetric relaxation, and mitral regurgitation removes isovolumetric contraction.

Jugular a is atrial contraction, c is tricuspid bulging, x is atrial relaxation and ring descent, v is atrial filling against a closed valve, and y is tricuspid opening; cannon a waves mean AV dissociation.
Inspiration delays P2; RBBB and pulmonic stenosis widen the split, ASD fixes it, and LBBB or aortic stenosis reverse it.
S3 is rapid filling of a volume-loaded ventricle and can be normal in the young; S4 is atrial contraction into a stiff ventricle and is absent in atrial fibrillation.

Stenosis is heard when a valve should be open and regurgitation when it should be closed; lower preload softens most murmurs but intensifies hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and makes the mitral valve prolapse click earlier.

verify: Auscultation areas: the tricuspid area is given as the left 4th or 5th intercostal space at the lower left sternal border in different texts; confirm the wording NABNE expects.

Resting pressures, volumes, ejection fraction range (55% to 70%), and the atrial contribution to filling (about 20% at rest, quoted from 15% to 30%) differ slightly between sources and are stated as approximate.
Peak LV pressures in severe aortic stenosis (about 180 to 250 mmHg) are illustrative; values vary with severity and output.
The sternal angle to right atrium distance (about 5 cm) and the upper limit of normal jugular venous height (about 3 cm above the sternal angle) vary slightly between clinical texts.
The normal inspiratory S2 split (about 0.04 s) and the threshold for an audible split (about 0.03 s) are approximate and vary between sources.
The age above which an S3 is considered pathologic is usually given as about 40 years; confirm the cutoff NABNE uses.
Pregnancy increases in blood volume (about 40% to 50%) and cardiac output (about 30% to 50%) are consensus ranges; confirm figures if tested.
Effect of handgrip on the aortic stenosis murmur (softer) is standard physiology but is omitted from some review tables; confirm NABNE expectations.
Prevalence of bicuspid aortic valve (about 1% to 2%) and the usual timing of papillary muscle rupture (within the first week) vary between sources.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: wiggers-diagram (LA, LV, and aortic pressures, LV volume, ECG, and heart sounds), pv-loop (normal loop with corners labeled and overlays for AS, AR, and MR), jvp-waveform (a, c, v waves and x, y descents timed to S1 and S2), s2-splitting (A2 and P2 timing in inspiration and expiration for each pattern), and murmur-timing (shapes of the main murmurs between S1 and S2).
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponym Still murmur or only the descriptive term.
